summary: "Kruunun-perämies" by Larin-Kyösti is a collection of short stories written in the early 20th century. It portrays the rough, comic, and often grim life of Finland’s outer islands—fishermen, pilots, smugglers, and petty officials battling the sea, poverty, and each other. The title story centers on Julius Sam Johnson, a mighty but wounded “crown mate” whose grief, drink, and pride clash with island temptations and a cunning housekeeper, Pirkko. The opening of the collection follows Julius Sam Johnson, a boisterous island constable who informally “taxes” smugglers, despises customs men, and drinks hard after his beloved wife’s death. Around him, the archipelago bustles with beach “courts,” anchor-salvage schemes, feasts, and pranks, while Pirkko and her accomplice Saska the signalman plot to fleece him, even faking a pregnancy and stealing his goods. Jealous brawls and a grotesque party—complete with a humiliated customs officer—push Sam toward ruin; Pirkko vanishes overseas with his money, and Sam, staggering between bravado and remorse, dreams of a final “harbor” before his house catches fire and he dies.
